items.title: AI-supported digital infrastructures in human health chemical risk assessment: recommendations from a joint VHP4Safety/ONTOX workshop
items.abstract: Chemical risk assessment is undergoing a fundamental transition driven by the need for human-relevant, mechanistically informed, and animal-free approaches. Digital infrastructures that integrate New Approach Methodologies (NAMs), including computational models and emerging artificial intelligence (AI) tools, are increasingly considered drivers of this transition. However, their regulatory uptake depends on several factors, including trust, transparency, scientific validity, and the sustainability of the infrastructures. This paper summarises the outcomes from a multi-stakeholder expert workshop, jointly organised by the European Centre for Ecotoxicology and Toxicology of Chemicals (ECETOC), the VHP4Safety project, and the ONTOX project, focusing on the application of AI-supported digital infrastructures in human health risk assessment of chemicals. The workshop explored technical, regulatory, and governance challenges associated with the integration of AI-supported NAMs into regulatory workflows. This was achieved through demonstrations of two recently developed platforms, the Virtual Human Platform (VHP) and Ontology-driven Probabilistic Risk Assessment (OPRA). Key insights highlight that transparency, traceability and explainability tailored to user needs are necessary for adoption and regulatory acceptance, as well as sustained engagement with regulators. Participants emphasised the importance of platform interoperability, and the need for targeted training for end users. Furthermore, long-term sustainability of digital infrastructures emerged as a critical concern, requiring distinct governance beyond project-based funding. Based on these insights, actionable recommendations for the design, implementation, and governance of AI-supported digital infrastructures to enable regulatory uptake of NAMs are reported. These recommendations are intended to inform developers, regulators and stakeholders advancing next-generation chemical risk assessment across regulatory domains.

items.title: AI, Bias, and Inclusion: A Two-Phase Mixed-Methods Study of Gender Bias, Awareness, and Trust in Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are widespread across fields such as healthcare, finance, employment, and criminal justice, with a substantial impact on the lives of individuals and society. However, it has been established that AI systems perpetuate existing social inequalities, particularly through biases that are not easily discernible. Such biases are embedded in the technical and social structures of artificial intelligence systems, making them difficult to detect. These biases challenge the concept of Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion (EDI), which recognizes diversity as the acknowledgment of individual differences, equity as fairness and equal access, and inclusion as the value placed on all participants. This study argues that fairness in artificial intelligence systems cannot be achieved by focusing solely on their technical aspects, necessitating a holistic approach. This study employs a two-phase mixed-methods design. Phase 1 applies computational content analysis to 360 occupational narratives generated by ChatGPT across four countries (Canada, Germany, India, and Bangladesh) using gender-neutral prompts to examine whether professions are predominantly associated with one gender and whether these patterns remain consistent across regions. Phase 2 examines the extent to which students recognize potential bias in AI, their trust in AI for consequential decision-making, and how these perceptions relate to themes in EDI and AI ethics scholarship. By combining output-level bias analysis with user perception data, this study identifies the empirical foundations necessary for future EDI-AI co-design frameworks, outlining the sociotechnical dimensions that such frameworks must address to be effective.

items.title: Algorithmic Management in Australian Workplaces: A Study on Transparency, Accountability and Worker Protection in AI-Driven Employment Decisions
items.abstract: AI systems are widely used in recruitment screening, job allocation, performance evaluation, remuneration decisions, promotion and dismissal. Compared with traditional human management, algorithmic management can improve information-processing efficiency and assist employers in making complex workplace decisions. This article employs doctrinal legal analysis to examine the regulation of AI-driven employment decisions under the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth), anti-discrimination law and the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth). Drawing on Mobley v Workday Inc and Houston Federation of Teachers v Houston Independent School District, it identifies the practical limitations of the existing legal framework. The analysis finds that Australian law provides partial protection, but remains fragmented and reactive. Workers generally obtain remedies only after an adverse decision has occurred, while the current framework lacks adequate pre-deployment disclosure, risk assessment, independent auditing and meaningful human review. It recommends prior disclosure, individualised reasons for adverse decisions, restrictions on solely automated decisions, clear employer accountability, algorithmic impact assessments, periodic independent audits and worker participation. These reforms would not prohibit workplace AI; rather, they would establish a more appropriate balance between technological efficiency, fairness, accountability and worker protection.

items.title: An Agent-Based Modeling Framework Integrating Social Behavior into GIS Digital Twins for Smart Disaster Management
items.abstract: Natural hazards are not purely physical phenomena but coupled human–environment systems in which consequences are shaped by behavioral, infrastructural, and institutional dynamics interacting with physical processes. While current Geographic Information System (GIS)-based digital twins, enhanced by artificial intelligence (AI), have advanced our capacity to monitor and predict physical hazard dynamics, they leave the social and behavioral dimensions of disaster largely unrepresented. This gap in situational intelligence constitutes a critical failure in smart disaster management, such as evacuation gridlock, warning non-compliance, and cascading infrastructure failures triggered by human decisions. This chapter discusses Cognitive Spatial Intelligence Systems (CSIS) as a new framework that addresses this gap by integrating five intelligence layers: Spatial Intelligence (GIS), System Intelligence (digital twins), Predictive Intelligence (AI and machine learning), Social Behavioral Intelligence (agent-based modeling, ABM), and Decision Intelligence (Environmental Decision Support Tools, EDST). Each layer answers a distinct scientific question that the others cannot resolve: where, what is happening, what will happen, how will people and systems respond, and what should we do. The chapter traces the evolution of spatial intelligence from static cartography through digital twins to CSIS; argues for ABM as the behavioral simulation engine for coupled human–environment hazard systems; and grounds the framework in the California wildfire system as a case study. This framework lets emergency managers anticipate behavioral responses, including evacuation decisions, traffic bottlenecks, warning compliance, and physical hazard forecasts. Integrating social simulation into operational digital twins will shift disaster management from reactive response toward active, behavior-aware decision support.

items.title: An Empirical Study on the Use Behavior for Healthcare Professionals to Utilize ChatGPT to Support Clinical Work
items.abstract: In the medical field, healthcare professionals often need to diagnose and treat patients based on their descriptions and disease characteristics. During this process, ChatGPT can serve as an auxiliary tool, offering professional advice and supporting clinical decisions. After treating patients, healthcare professionals typically need to provide follow-up health education, such as explaining diagnoses, prescriptions, treatment plans, and necessary precautions. ChatGPT can handle these tasks on their behalf. Utilizing the UTAUT2 model framework, this study incorporates additional variables such as trust, privacy risks, salary, and education level to understand the factors influencing healthcare professionals' willingness to use ChatGPT for job assistance. Surveys were conducted among healthcare professionals serving in medical institutions at the regional level and above, and data was analyzed using descriptive statistics and structural equation modeling. The study results can serve as a reference for healthcare institutions planning to implement relevant information technologies.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Adoption and Journalistic Practice in Nigeria: Examining Professional Competence, Ethical Challenges and News Credibility
items.abstract: This study examined artificial intelligence (AI) adoption and journalistic practice in Nigeria, focusing on professional competence, ethical challenges and journalists’ perceptions of news credibility. A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted among practising journalists across print, broadcast and digital media organisations. Data from 392 respondents were analysed using descriptive statistics, Cronbach’s alpha reliability analysis, Pearson’s product-moment correlation and multiple regression. AI applications were most commonly used for grammar checking and editing (77.0%), content generation (73.0%) and automated transcription (69.1%). Respondents reported moderate-to-high perceived professional competence (M = 3.48), alongside comparatively lower scores for identifying inaccuracies and independently verifying AI-generated information. Ethical challenges were rated highly (M = 4.04), particularly inadequate organisational guidelines, misinformation risks and excessive dependence on AI. Journalists’ perceived news credibility score was also high (M = 4.08), reflecting strong support for human editorial supervision, independent fact-checking and transparency. The regression model showed professional competence as a positive predictor and ethical challenges as a negative predictor of journalists’ perceived news credibility. The study concludes that responsible AI integration requires continuous professional training, institutional ethical guidelines and strengthened editorial oversight.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Business Management: A Framework For AI-Assisted Decision-Making
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) can support business managers by forecasting demand, identifying operational exceptions, andsummarizing information. Its contribution depends on how firms incorporate these outputs into decisions and assess theconsequences. This article develops a framework for AI-assisted decision-making through a conceptual synthesis of selected research on organizational decision structures, AI capabilities, and workplace productivity. The framework comprises four stages: defining the business decision and its baseline, assigning decision authority, piloting AI in the workflow, and evaluating business outcomes before expanding its use. An illustrative inventory replenishment case demonstrates how forecast accuracy, managerial overrides, and service levels can be assessed together. The case shows why an improvement in forecast accuracy can leave ordering decisions unchanged and why lower stockout rates should be evaluated alongside inventory costs. The article’s contribution is to connect AI implementation to decision accountability and measurable operational outcomes. The framework requires empirical validation across business functions and organizational settings.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in IT Project Management: A Critical Analysis of Benefits, Challenges, and Risk Management Strategies
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is revolutionizing information technology (IT) project management with intelligent automation, predictive analytics, and data-driven project decisions over project lifecycles. Nevertheless, even though AI may enhance operational efficiency, the implementation of this technology has witnessed technological, organizational, and ethical issues, which can cripple the impact of a project. This paper has critically analyzed the advantages and limitations of the use of AI in IT project management with a particular interest in the implications of AI for technical project managers and performance in organizations. An ordered literature review and thematic synthesis of the related publications on IEEE Xplore are suggested to analyze the existing evidence on AI-based scheduling, resource allocation, risk prediction, and project governance. Special consideration is made for relationships such as technological capabilities, organizational readiness, data quality, and human oversight. The article further addresses the issue of whether the enhancement of operational efficiency will inevitably lead to the sustainability of project success, in particular, when the complexity of integration, bias in algorithms, the problem of cybersecurity, and labour constraints are not well managed. The research seeks to bridge these dimensions in order to come up with an evidence-based framework, which would direct responsible AI adoption within the management of IT projects. It is expected to provide a better understanding of the conditions in which AI may be used to assist in the delivery of a project, without jeopardizing managerial responsibility, transparency, and organizational control.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Medicine: Methodologies, Clinical Applications, Challenges, and Future Perspectives
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being investigated as a means of improving the collection, interpretation, and use of health information. Applications range from image based diagnosis and clinical risk prediction to workflow support, drug discovery, remote monitoring, and population health. This narrative review examines the methodological foundations of AI in medicine, summarizes representative clinical applications, and critically evaluates the conditions required for safe and equitable implementation. It distinguishes conventional machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, computer vision, and generative AI, while emphasizing that the suitability of a method depends on the clinical question, data structure, intended user, and consequences of error. Evidence from retinal imaging, dermatology, breast cancer screening, and health system prediction illustrates both the promise and the limitations of algorithmic systems. Across these domains, high performance in retrospective datasets does not automatically demonstrate improved patient outcomes. External validation, calibration, prospective evaluation, workflow integration, monitoring for data drift, and clear accountability are essential. Ethical concerns include privacy, informed consent, bias, unequal access, automation bias, explainability, and the environmental and institutional costs of deployment. International guidance and reporting standards, including WHO guidance, CONSORT AI, SPIRIT AI, DECIDE AI, and TRIPOD+AI, provide useful structures for governance and transparent research. The review concludes that AI should be treated as a sociotechnical clinical intervention rather than a stand alone software product. Its most defensible role is to augment appropriately trained healthcare professionals, improve access and consistency where validated, and support rather than replace clinical judgment and patient centred care.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Literacy of College Students and Their Ethical Utilization
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) offers opportunities for learning in higher education while raising concerns about academic integrity, privacy, bias, and misinformation. This study examined AI literacy and ethical AI utilization among second-year Bachelor of Secondary Education major in Science students at City College of Calapan and investigated their relationship as a basis for proposing an institutional framework. A quantitative descriptive-correlational design was employed, involving 43 respondents purposively selected from a population of 48 students. Data were analyzed using weighted means and Pearson’s correlation coefficient. Findings revealed high AI literacy in technical knowledge (M = 2.77) and prompting (M = 2.58), but low literacy in critical evaluation (M = 2.42). Ethical utilization was rated low across academic integrity compliance (M = 1.82), ethical awareness and data privacy (M = 2.17), and bias and misinformation mitigation (M = 2.43). The overall relationship between AI literacy and ethical utilization was not statistically significant (r = −0.135, p = 0.389). However, technical knowledge demonstrated a significant moderate negative relationship with bias and misinformation mitigation (r = −0.458, p = 0.002). These findings suggest that technical competence alone does not necessarily translate into responsible AI use. Accordingly, an Institutional Artificial Intelligence Program and Policy Framework adapted from Bilgin’s responsible AI framework was proposed. It comprises AI literacy development, AI utilization policy, AI detection and support tools, monitoring and support, and ethical awareness. The framework emphasizes responsible, ethical, and competent AI utilization through institutional guidance, critical evaluation, academic accountability, and continuing development initiatives for students and faculty.

items.title: Artificial intelligence training labour and the training economy: How generative models reconfigure value extraction in the digital economy
items.abstract: This article theorises an emergent training economy in which selected forms of human cognitive, evaluative, corrective, annotative and creative activity become inputs into the training, alignment, evaluation, validation or optimisation of generative AI systems. It develops AI training labour as the analytical category naming these contributions across contracted, precarious and unrecognised arrangements, with particular attention to weakly compensated or institutionally obscured activity. Drawing on digital labour theory, platform political economy and critical data studies, the article argues that generative AI reconfigures platform capitalism by creating a productive route through which selected digital participation can contribute to model development alongside advertising, subscription, cloud and rent-based accumulation. It distinguishes three evidentiary statuses: documented, where technical incorporation is publicly established; inferred, where a credible incorporation pathway exists but actual use is not independently confirmed; and governance risk, where disclosure is insufficient to determine whether incorporation occurs. These are analytically separate from labour status, which ranges from contracted and paid to unpaid and unrecognised. The argument is probed across routine interface interaction, creative production and educational deployment. The training economy proposition specifies the conditions under which human interaction becomes an appropriable input into AI productive capacity, and identifies supporting and disconfirming evidence. Advanced as a tendency rather than a settled regime, the framework connects micro-level labour relations to value extraction, infrastructural concentration and governance in AI-driven digital economies.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Green Recruitment Practices and Their Impact on Employee Engagement and Retention: An Empirical Study of Sustainable Human Resource Management
items.abstract: This study examines the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Green Recruitment Practices and its impact on employee engagement and retention. Integrating AI with Green Human Resource Management enables organizations to digitize recruitment, reduce paper consumption, minimize unnecessary travel, improve candidate screening and matching, and communicate sustainability-oriented employment values. AI can support candidate sourcing, resume screening, virtual assessments, interview scheduling, candidate communication and recruitment analytics. However, organizations must also address concerns relating to fairness, transparency, privacy, algorithmic bias and excessive automation. Following the structure of the supplied model paper, the present study adopts a quantitative approach using a structured questionnaire and an illustrative sample of 300 respondents. Frequency analysis, Chi-square, ANOVA, correlation, and multiple regression are used to examine the relationships among AI-enabled green recruitment practices, employee engagement, and retention. The illustrative findings indicate significant associations between AI-enabled green recruitment and employee engagement and retention intention. Fairness and transparency, perceived environmental responsibility and employee engagement also emerge as important factors associated with retention. The study recommends human oversight, transparent AI governance, monitoring of algorithmic bias, responsible data management, digital, paperless recruitment, and alignment between recruitment promises and actual green organizational practices. The study concludes that AI can strengthen Green Recruitment Practices and contribute to employee engagement and retention when technological efficiency is combined with authentic sustainability and responsible HR management.

items.title: Artificial intelligence, new product development, and design: Towards a framework for artificial intelligence adoption in innovation research
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) plays an increasingly central role in organizations’ digital transformation. There is growing scholarly interest in how AI supports innovation, that is, how activities and processes aimed at producing novel ideas, problem solutions or other outputs can be enabled by autonomous machines. This article focuses on the role of AI in new product development (NPD) and aims to develop theoretical insights into how AI is reshaping innovation processes. In a systematic review of 1,192 articles published in business and management journals between 1993 and 2024, we identified 67 relevant to AI, NPD, and design. Through a focus on design activities, choices and results, we analyse how AI has been adopted in NPD processes. We find that AI can help manage design complexity and relax traditional constraints, evidencing an alignment with theoretical frameworks centered on process and methodology; at the same time, current adoption of AI in NPD remains largely focused on the implementation and pursuit of measurable performance outcomes. By integrating our findings with existing innovation and AI literatures, we propose an integrative framework that builds on three pillars—strategic orientation, collaboration architecture, and value optimization—and sheds light on the role of governance as a meta‐level coordination mechanism.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence: Innovative Tools for Idea Registration and Evaluation
items.abstract: Suggestion systems play an important role in encouraging employee participation, improving organizational processes, fostering innovation, and enhancing productivity. However, traditional suggestion systems often face challenges such as the accumulation of unevaluated ideas, repetitive submissions, lengthy evaluation procedures, and a lack of transparent and integrated assessment mechanisms.This presentation explores how artificial intelligence can transform organizational suggestion systems, covering the entire process from idea registration and enrichment to preliminary screening, analysis, and evaluation. It first introduces AI-powered assistants that can convert raw notes and initial ideas into structured proposals, enrich technical and economic information through interactive questioning, identify similar or duplicate submissions, and connect new ideas to the organization's existing knowledge and previous experiences.The presentation then examines the intelligent idea evaluation cycle, including preliminary screening, multi-criteria scoring, impact simulation, and hybrid decision-making. Particular attention is given to AI agents designed to identify similar proposals, analyze supporting documents and evidence, assign preliminary scores based on approved criteria and weights, identify strengths and weaknesses, and flag proposals requiring further technical, financial, or legal assessment by experts.In the practical section, an AI-powered Idea Evaluation Agent is introduced, and its application is demonstrated through the analysis of a sample organizational proposal. The presentation also highlights essential requirements for successful implementation, including data confidentiality, algorithmic transparency, integration with organizational knowledge management systems, and maintaining human oversight in final decision-making.The main objective is to demonstrate how artificial intelligence can transform traditional, administrative suggestion systems into intelligent, transparent, and effective mechanisms that convert employees' ideas into organizational value and innovation.

items.title: Ask or Act: A Calibrated-Confidence Framework for Risk-Aware Navigation Under Uncertain Human Intent
items.abstract: Mobile robots that share space with people must decide within seconds whether a pedestrian is about to cross their path, and confidence-based rules that ask the person only when unsure promise to combine safety with efficiency. Such rules are only as safe as their predicted probabilities, yet calibration is usually fitted and evaluated over all available samples, most of which come from moments far from any decision, and its closed-loop effect under distribution shift is rarely tested. We present Ask or Act, a framework in which a robot predicts the probability that a pedestrian will cross, calibrates it, and at a decision deadline yields, proceeds or asks. We propose decision-aware calibration, fitted only on the window in which the robot decides, and evaluate it with a TurtleBot3 in ROS~2 and Gazebo, using eight scripted pedestrian behaviors with known intent under five distribution shifts and a pre-specified analysis plan on held-out scenarios. Under degraded tracking, raw and conventionally recalibrated confidence led to collisions in 34.5% and 15.5% of crossing encounters, against 1.3% with decision-aware recalibration, which remained the safer method for all five predictors trained with different seeds (1.3-10.5% against 5.5-15.8%). Under nominal conditions it asked 16% fewer questions than always asking, within a pre-set non-inferiority margin. Offline results agreed with Gazebo in 97.5% of paired episodes, and the pipeline ran on the robot's onboard computer in about per step. For robots that act on predicted probabilities, calibration should be fitted and evaluated where decisions are made.

items.title: Auditing the Judge: Human-Derived Bias Discovery, Quantification, and Mitigation in LLM Judges
items.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as automated evaluators in evaluation and training pipelines, their judgements are often affected by systematic biases that conflict with human preferences. Although prior work has identified various biases and proposed methods for detecting and mitigating them, less attention has been paid to using human preferences to inform bias identification and mitigation. Moreover, these approaches rely heavily on pre-discovered bias lists, overlook bias strength, and depend on costly interventions. In this work, we propose HUB-J, an integrated framework based on human-derived bias factors that detects, quantifies, and mitigates biases in LLM-as-a-Judge systems. Our approach leverages human-LLM judgement disagreement cases to automatically discover interpretable bias factors, and utilizes agreement cases to quantify bias strength through controlled input modifications and resulting shifts in model decisions. Finally, building on these quantified biases, we introduce a lightweight, training-free regression-based mitigation strategy that estimates the influence of each bias factor on model judgments and corrects bias-influenced decisions by removing its estimated effect. Empirical results show that HUB-J uncovers both known and novel bias factors, reveals meaningful differences in model susceptibility, and consistently reduces bias-driven decision flips while generalizing across models.

items.title: Augmented With AI: Practical Guide for Clinician Educators Engaged in Health Professions Education Scholarship
items.abstract: Clinician educators occupy a demanding role at the intersection of clinical practice, teaching, and scholarship. Given their teaching roles, they are expected to contribute in particular to health professions education scholarship, yet many have little protected time. AI tools have emerged as practical support for 2 of the time-intensive aspects of scholarly activities: conducting early-stage literature reviews and improving scholarly writing. The rapidly expanding AI landscape has made it increasingly difficult to distinguish purpose-built scholarly platforms from general-purpose AI assistants. As a result, many clinician educators remain uncertain about which tools are appropriate for academic work and how they can be used responsibly. Additionally, the barriers are often as much institutional as individual. Limited protected time, access to experienced mentors, methodological expertise, editorial support, and library services all shape the ability of clinician educators to engage in scholarship. Although AI tools may reduce some of the burdens associated with literature review and writing, they should not be viewed as substitutes for these institutional supports. This viewpoint is intended for clinician educators seeking practical guidance on integrating AI into health professions education scholarship. Our aim is not to provide a systematic review, an exhaustive list of platforms, or an endorsement or ranking of any platform, but rather to offer a practical overview of selected AI tools that we have found useful for health professions education research. These tools include Consensus, Elicit, Scite, Litmaps, ResearchRabbit, Paperpal, Jenni AI, Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, and Microsoft Copilot. We group these tools into 6 functional categories and discuss their strengths and limitations across different stages of the scholarly workflow, drawing on vendor documentation and our own experience rather than formal comparative testing, while emphasizing the importance of selecting tools that align with specific scholarly tasks. Since overreliance on AI risks diminishing creative scholarly competencies, we distinguish productive cognitive support, in which AI reduces routine workload, from epistemic off-loading, in which interpretation and judgment are delegated to AI, and argue for using AI as a scaffold that enhances, rather than replaces, intellectual engagement. We also address some ethical considerations, including hallucinated content, citation inaccuracies, transparency in disclosure, and subscription costs. Ultimately, responsible integration of AI into scholarship will require not only appropriate tool selection but also the continued cultivation of the critical thinking and scientific reasoning that define academic scholarship.

items.title: Authors' Response to AI-Based Reviews: A Mixed-Methods Pilot Study
items.abstract: Background: Large language models are increasingly used to assist scholarly peer review, but there is limited evidence about how authors judge their feedback and use it to revise their papers. Methods: We studied authors' experiences of receiving an auxiliary AI review alongside human reviews in three computer-science cohorts: LifeCLEF 2025, LifeCLEF 2026, and CVWW 2026. Post-review questionnaires yielded 92 responses concerning 71 papers. We summarized closed-ended answers using descriptive statistics and examined free-text responses through thematic analysis. Results: Most responses rated the AI review useful (82/92 (89%), and 82/92 (89%) reported using at least some of its suggestions in revision. Authors reported that AI identified issues missed by human reviewers ((76/92 (83%). However, 44/92 (48%) trusted AI feedback less than human feedback, and 58/92 (63%) reported incorrect or misleading comments. Authors valued suggestions that improved clarity and reproducibility, but also described overlooked evidence, inappropriate demands, and difficulty finding useful comments within lengthy reviews. They emphasized the need to check AI feedback and retain control over how their manuscripts were processed. Future review by both humans and AI was supported by 85/92 (92%); 83/92 (90%) preferred advance notice and 73/92 (79%) supported explicit consent. Conclusions: Authors often found AI reviews useful for revision without trusting them as much as human reviews. These exploratory findings favor a supplementary role for AI, with human oversight, clear disclosure, and author consent. They do not establish that AI can replace human reviewers or improve manuscript quality.

items.title: Between cognitive scaffolding and creative agency: A semester-long qualitative study of pre-service EFL teachers’ engagement with ChatGPT
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT are rapidly entering language teacher education, yet little is known about how pre-service teachers negotiate these tools during authentic instructional planning over time. Drawing on distributed cognition and a mini-c/little-c account of pedagogical creativity, this qualitative study examined how pre-service English as a foreign language (EFL) teachers perceived and negotiated ChatGPT's role in lesson design, critical evaluation, and collaborative reflection across one semester. Twenty-four senior pre-service teachers at a Turkish state university, all completing a school practicum, submitted weekly reflective narratives (n = 232) and took part in end-of-semester semi-structured interviews (n = 24). The data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. Six themes were constructed: pedagogical affordances; perceived pedagogical and cognitive risks; human-AI co-creation; epistemic evaluation and validation routines; collaborative reflection and peer scaffolding; and recommendations for teacher education. Participants did not describe ChatGPT as a source of creativity in itself; rather, they located pedagogical creativity in their own iterative constraining, rejecting, and localizing of AI output. At the same time, they reported that offloading pedagogical reasoning, as opposed to routine production, weakened both their planning and its classroom enactment. Verification of AI output was frequently collective, taking place in peer and mentor debriefings. The study offers an account of how novice teachers described negotiating the division of cognitive labor with GenAI and derives three data-grounded implications for language teacher education: assessing design processes rather than products alone, auditing AI output for accuracy and bias, and teaching iterative co-design.

items.title: Beyond Adoption: Extending the Theory of Planned Behavior to Explain Ethical Use of Generative AI among Indonesian University Students
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has become pervasive in students’ academic activities, yet the mechanisms linking acceptance, ethical concern, and actual use remain underexplored in non-Western higher education contexts. This study extends the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) by incorporating AI-related ethical concern as an additional predictor and tests the resulting model on GenAI use among Indonesian university students. A cross-sectional online survey was conducted with 560 students who had prior GenAI experience, and the data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. The findings show that students mainly used GenAI for initial information searches, literature-source searches, concept clarification, and academic document analysis. Perceived behavioral control was the strongest predictor of behavioral intention, followed by attitude. Subjective norms were not significant, whereas AI-related ethical concern had a small but significant negative effect. Behavioral intention was positively associated with self-reported actual GenAI use. The model explained 45.7% of the variance in behavioral intention and 23.9% of actual behavior. Overall, the findings suggest that perceived behavioral control and attitude are the primary correlates of GenAI-use intention, whereas AI-related ethical concern provides only a small additional restraint signal. The results emphasize the importance of AI literacy, clear task-level guidance, and ethical self-efficacy in higher education while warranting cautious interpretation given the cross-sectional and self-reported nature of the data.

items.title: BEYOND AI RECOMMENDATIONS: INTEGRATING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE, CRITICAL THINKING AND HUMAN GUIDANCE IN SECONDARY SCHOOL CAREER DEVELOPMENT
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is expanding access to occupational information, educational pathways and personalized exploration in career guidance. However, AI-generated recommendations do not necessarily lead to informed, autonomous or responsible career decisions, particularly among secondary-school students whose interests, identities and decision-making competencies are still developing. This paper proposed the AI–Critical Thinking–Human Guidance (AI–CT–HG) framework, an original conceptual model for integrating AI-supported exploration, critical thinking and human guidance in secondary school career development. The framework comprises five interconnected stages: self-awareness, AI-supported exploration, critical evaluation, reflective human dialogue, and informed decision-making followed by action and review. It was developed through a conceptual synthesis of literature on career construction, planned happenstance, critical thinking, AI in education and human-centred AI governance. The model positions AI as an exploratory resource rather than an authority that determines career choices. Critical thinking serves as the mechanism for evaluating generated information, identifying uncertainty and comparing alternatives, while human guidance provides contextual interpretation, ethical oversight and support for student agency. Transparency, privacy, fairness, accessibility and accountability operate as cross-cutting principles. Practical implications include a structured school-based learning sequence and proposed indicators for assessing the quality of students’ career reasoning. Because the framework has not yet been empirically tested, the paper provides a conceptual foundation for pilot studies and evaluation in diverse educational settings.

items.title: Beyond automation: How AI implementation transforms middle manager roles in banking compliance
items.abstract: Type of the article: Research ArticleMajed Salem Alsuhaimi - Corresponding author, email: suhaimims@kfsc.edu.saAbstractArtificial intelligence deployment in banking compliance represents one of the most significant workplace transformations in financial services, yet scholarly understanding of how middle managers navigate this transformation remains limited. This qualitative study examines how 18 middle managers across three Saudi banks experienced and adapted to AI-driven role change. Using theory-informed abductive analysis grounded in organizational role theory, the research identifies structural role ambiguity – existential uncertainty about whether roles persist in recognizable form following technological implementation – as theoretically distinctive from traditional role ambiguity.Key findings demonstrate that 89% of participants experienced structural role ambiguity, 83% engaged in active multi-stakeholder role negotiation across organizational hierarchies, 78% employed strategic framing to position AI as augmentation rather than replacement, and all 18 experienced compressed implementation timelines (4-6 months). Compressed implementation velocity functioned as a contextual condition: rapid deployment intensified initial ambiguity through overwhelming organizational simultaneity while paradoxically accelerating resolution through forcing mechanisms.Theoretically, the study makes four contributions to organizational role theory: identifying structural role ambiguity as theoretically distinctive; demonstrating multi-stakeholder rather than dyadic role negotiation; showing that managers exercise significant agency through strategic framing; and clarifying how implementation shapes role transformation temporal dynamics. Empirically, the study provides an in-depth qualitative examination of AI’s impact on compliance professionals in compressed implementation contexts. Practically, the work identifies actionable competencies and strategic guidance for organizational stakeholders.

items.title: Beyond Giving Answers: Scaffolding Critical Thinking with Stage-Structured Generative AI Feedback in Introductory Programming
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence can support programming learning, but complete solutions may reduce opportunities to practice critical thinking. This study examined a pedagogical agent guided by the Trigger-Process-Respond framework, which organized questioning, comparison, evidence requests, and reflection across debugging, code review, and post-task reflection. In a six-week quasi-experiment, 60 first-year computer science students in two intact classes at a Chinese university completed three sequential programming tasks. One class used the agent, and the other received conventional instructor feedback. Critical thinking was assessed with the Chinese version of the California Critical Thinking Skills Test, and dialogue records documented students’ reasoning responses. In these two classes, the agent-supported class had higher posttest scores after adjustment for pretest scores. Within the fixed feedback sequences, questioning was followed by more analytical responses, comparison by more evaluative responses, and evidence requests by more argumentative responses. Exploratory analyses linked reflection feedback with reasoning in the next task, particularly between the first two tasks. These findings suggest that stage-structured generative AI feedback can engage students in reasoning during supported programming dialogue.

items.title: Beyond Prompting: Student–GenAI Interaction and Critical Thinking in STEM Education—A Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is becoming increasingly common in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) education, but its role in students’ critical thinking (CT) remains unclear. This systematic literature review examines how students interact with GenAI, the factors influencing these interactions, and their relationships with CT-related processes in STEM learning. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we searched Scopus, Web of Science, and IEEE Xplore and identified 204 records, of which 17 empirical studies met the inclusion criteria. Six clusters of CT-related processes were found through narrative and thematic synthesis: strategic questioning and task framing; interpretation and analytical decomposition; comparison, evaluation, and verification; error detection and corrective modification; justification, judgment, and independent decision-making; and reflection, metacognition, and self-regulation. Across the included studies, interactions involving questioning AI-generated solutions, verifying their accuracy, examining alternatives, and revising initial interpretations were associated with CT-related processes. Conversely, reliance on GenAI to perform essential reasoning tasks or uncritical acceptance of AI-generated responses may limit opportunities for independent reasoning. These findings suggest that the nature of student–GenAI interactions, particularly the extent to which students retain cognitive responsibility, is important for understanding how GenAI relates to CT processes. Based on the synthesis, we propose an evidence-informed conceptual framework that links student–GenAI interactions, cognitive responsibility, and CT-related processes with personal, instructional, and task-related factors. The framework is derived from the reviewed evidence and requires further empirical validation. However, methodological heterogeneity and limited direct measurement of independent CT outcomes prevent definitive conclusions about whether GenAI improves students’ critical-thinking ability. The review highlights the importance of designing STEM learning activities that encourage questioning, verification, reflection, and independent judgment when interacting with GenAI. Further experimental and longitudinal research is needed to validate the proposed framework and examine how student–GenAI interactions influence critical-thinking development over time.

items.title: Beyond the Paycheck: What Sustains Employee Motivation in High-Income Economies?
items.abstract: Rich economies pay well, yet most of their employees are not engaged. Gallup’s 2026 global survey puts engagement at 20% worldwide and at 12% in Europe, against 31% in the United States and Canada. This paper asks what, besides pay, sustains motivation where pay is already high. It combines secondary analysis of public data with a structured synthesis of meta-analyses and large surveys. Across 18 high-income countries whose income per head differs by a factor of 3.4, national income was unrelated to engagement (Spearman ρ = 0.22, permutation p = .37; 0.8 percentage points per doubling of income, 95% CI − 6.8 to 8.5), and among 14 European countries the correlation was − 0.03. Regions dominated by high-income economies score far higher on life evaluation (52% thriving against 31%) but not on engagement (21% against 22%). Pay level correlates only .15 with job satisfaction, explaining about 2% of its variance, whereas motivational and social work characteristics explain 34% and a further 17%. Pay is nonetheless not trivial: 63% of Americans who quit in 2021 cited low pay (95% CI 60% to 66%), as often as lack of advancement and more often than feeling disrespected (57%). Intrinsic motivation predicts performance (ρ = .21 to .45, k = 183), while financial incentives add most for the quantity of output, and a four-day week at unchanged pay reduced burnout from 2.83 to 2.38 on a five-point scale. Pay works as a threshold and a signal of fairness. Beyond it, motivation is sustained by work design, meaning, respect, development and control of time. The evidence is cross-sectional and uneven in quality, and the paper says where it is thin.

items.title: Calm Agent: Reframing Agent Interaction around Intermittent Human Attention
items.abstract: AI agents can carry out auxiliary tasks while users focus on other work. Yet users still need to understand task state, make changes, and respond when help is required. We argue that agents for ongoing auxiliary tasks should be designed around intermittent human attention: tasks should continue between interactions, and users should be able to return with little effort to understand and control them. We develop this position as Calm Agent. It connects three on-demand interaction modes: Delegate, Adjust, and Check, through a persistent task representation. Generative interaction provides controls and feedback suited to open-ended goals, while existing controls support routine actions. We illustrate these principles with Orvlet, a desktop prototype for background execution and compact task interfaces. We identify challenges in adapting interfaces while preserving continuity, coordinating attention across tasks, providing responsive interaction, and learning user habits over time. The aim is to support continuing task control while protecting attention for primary work.

items.title: Can Artificial Intelligence Support Multigrade Teaching?: Exploring Teachers’ Perceptions, Practices, and Challenges
items.abstract: Multigrade teachers face unique instructional challenges as they simultaneously manage learners from different grade levels, particularly in rural school settings where access to educational resources and technology is often limited. Although artificial intelligence (AI) has increasingly been recognized as a potential tool for enhancing teaching and learning, limited research has explored how multigrade teachers in rural Philippine classrooms perceive, utilize, and navigate the integration of AI into their instructional practices. Addressing this gap, this study explored the perceptions, practices, perceived benefits, challenges, and support needs of multigrade teachers in integrating AI into their teaching. A qualitative case study approach was employed, involving ten (10) multigrade teachers from Kadingilan II District, Division of Bukidnon, during School Year 2026–2027. Data were gathered through semi-structured interviews, focus group discussions, and classroom observations. The findings revealed that teachers perceived AI as a supportive instructional assistant rather than a replacement for their professional roles. Based on their experiences, AI helped facilitate lesson preparation, differentiated instruction, and assessment. However, they emphasized that teacher judgment, creativity, and personal interaction with learners remain essential. The major challenges identified included limited internet connectivity, inaccuracies in AI-generated materials, cultural mismatches, and the risk of over-reliance on AI. To address these concerns, teachers practiced critical evaluation of AI-generated outputs, contextual adaptation of instructional materials, and peer collaboration. Furthermore, teachers identified practical, classroom-focused training, reliable internet connectivity, adequate technological devices, offline AI resources, and clear guidelines on ethical use, data privacy, and academic integrity as essential support mechanisms. The study concludes that AI has potential as a supplementary teaching tool in multigrade classrooms, particularly when supported by adequate resources, professional development, and responsible use. The reported benefits reflect teachers' experiences and perceptions rather than measured improvements in instructional effectiveness. These findings highlight the importance of context-responsive support in promoting meaningful and equitable AI integration in rural multigrade education.

items.title: Capability Is Not Authority: Decision Sovereignty and the Governance of Authority Delegated to AI Systems
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence systems move from informing decisions to taking actions, the central governance question shifts from what a system can do to what it may do. This paper argues that capability and authority are distinct and that institutions lose control when they treat one as the other. Capability is the power to do something and is possessed by the actor. Authority is the legitimate right to decide and act; it is granted, bounded, accountable and revocable. A system cannot create legitimate authority for itself, but it can acquire de facto control over outcomes that no one granted. The paper develops the principle of Decision Sovereignty, under which an institution, not the systems it deploys, owns its decisions and their execution. It introduces measurement constructs from the Decision Sovereignty Governance Methodology (DSGM): an eight-level A-scale; Permitted AI Authority (PAA) and Effective AI Authority (EAA), read on the same scale; the Authority Gap between them; and Choice Architecture Control (CAC), which captures a system's power over the options humans see. It traces a sequence of failure, from authority drift through judgment displacement and an accountability vacuum to legitimacy collapse, and sets out a governing discipline of six authority questions that together form an Authority Charter. The paper positions Authority Exposure as a risk category that complements the AI-First Risk Intelligence Framework (AIRIF™) and closes with testable propositions. This working paper presents the core argument of the author's forthcoming book, Capability Is Not Authority: Why Institutions Must Remain Sovereign Over the Systems They Deploy (AIRIF Press), and builds on AIRIF™: AI-First Risk Intelligence Framework (AIRIF Press, 2026; ISBN 979-8-9982544-0-6) and the author's earlier working paper (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24323708).

items.title: CIVIL LIABILITY FOR INCORRECT LEGAL ADVICE PROVIDED THROUGH ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE: UZBEKISTAN'S LEGISLATION AND FOREIGN EXPERIENCE
items.abstract: This article examines civil liability for damages caused to individuals as a result of incorrect, outdated, or unreliable legal advice provided through artificial intelligence (AI). It explores the specific characteristics of damage arising from AI-based legal services, the identification of liable parties, the challenges of establishing damage and causation, and the legal status of service providers, developers, legal professionals, and users. The civil legislation of the Republic of Uzbekistan and regulatory frameworks governing artificial intelligence are comparatively analyzed in light of international experience. Based on the findings, the article proposes a differential liability model aimed at allocating liability according to the functional roles, obligations, fault, and causal contribution of each party to the occurrence of damage. The proposed model distinguishes between the mechanism for compensating the injured party and the internal recourse relationships among the parties involved.

items.title: CollaGraph: Mediating Human-AI Co-Creation of Interactive Mathematical Visualization through Structured Shared Context
items.abstract: Interactive visualizations (IVs) for mathematics are valuable for explanation and self-exploration, but their creation presents challenges, particularly for inexperienced creators. We present CollaGraph, a human-AI collaborative system for IV creation. Informed by formative studies that highlight the importance of complex dependencies and dynamic processes in IV creation, we propose the Dynamic Reliance Graph (DRG) as a node-based structured representation of IVs and incorporate it into CollaGraph. In CollaGraph, human creators and AI collaboratively iterate on shared structured content, including design plan lists and DRGs, through direct editing and comments. By compiling DRGs into IV previews, CollaGraph highlights the connections among components of the design plan, DRG, and IV outcome, thereby supporting the creative cycle of verification and modification. items.title: Competency‑based and emotional predictors of pre‑service teachers’ orientation towards the responsible use of Generative AI
items.abstract: The integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into initial teacher education requires an understanding not only of how frequently these tools are used, but also of the factors that shape their responsible adoption. This study examines how pre‑service teachers’ orientation towards responsible GenAI use is configured, identifying the competency-based resources and usage‑related variables that underpin it, as well as the role of anxiety across the dimensions assessed. A total of 298 pre‑service teachers from two Spanish universities participated, completing a validated 25‑item instrument comprising five dimensions: attitudes towards the use of AI for employability, digital flow in the responsible and safe use of AI, creativity to use AI responsibly, anxiety about using AI in future work contexts, and responsible use of AI for employability. Robust group comparisons, hierarchical regressions, and a network analysis with hierarchical clustering were conducted. The confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) supported the instrument’s five‑factor structure. Creativity (β = 0.42) and digital flow (β = 0.37) emerged as the strongest predictors of responsible use, whereas usage frequency made no unique positive contribution. Anxiety was higher among women and younger participants; in the regression model it was associated with more favourable attitudes and higher digital flow, and with lower creativity only when these were controlled (a suppression effect). It occupied a peripheral position within the correlation network. The findings are synthesised in an exploratory two‑path empirical model that requires confirmatory testing. Initial teacher education may therefore benefit from fostering creative GenAI‑based experiences while deliberately addressing the emotional dimension of learning these technologies.

items.title: Computer Science and Engineering Students’ Acceptance of Generative AI for Programming: An Extended Technology Acceptance Model with Trust and Risk Perceptions
items.abstract: This study investigated factors associated with computer science and engineering students’ acceptance of generative AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, GitHub Copilot, Google Gemini) for programming tasks by extending the Technology Acceptance Model 2 (TAM2) with trust and perceived risk constructs. Using structural equation modeling with data from 304 undergraduate students across five universities in Turkey, the study examined the direct and indirect within-model associations of perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, subjective norms, image, TAM2 cognitive instrumental determinants (job relevance, output quality, results demonstrability), trust, and perceived risk with behavioral intention. The proposed model accounted for 51.6% of the variance in perceived usefulness and 45.9% in behavioral intention. Results revealed that perceived usefulness was the strongest direct predictor of behavioral intention, while perceived ease of use exhibited the largest total association with behavioral intention among exogenous variables through both direct and indirect pathways. Subjective norms significantly predicted perceived usefulness but were associated with behavioral intention only indirectly, a pattern consistent with an internalization rather than a compliance mechanism. Trust was not significantly associated with perceived risk. Perceived risk was negatively associated with perceived usefulness and was associated with behavioral intention only indirectly, through perceived usefulness. Notably, image and TAM2’s cognitive instrumental determinants (job relevance, output quality, results demonstrability) and trust did not significantly predict perceived usefulness, suggesting that traditional cognitive evaluation pathways may not transfer to non-deterministic AI technologies in educational contexts. These findings point to a risk-dominant acceptance pattern among technically literate students, in which higher risk perceptions are associated with lower perceived usefulness while trust shows no significant association with either usefulness or risk. Practical implications for educators, tool developers, and institutions seeking to support effective and responsible generative AI integration in programming education are discussed.

items.title: Consumer Adoption of AI-Powered Healthcare Product Recommendations: Examining Trust and Purchase Intention in Uttarakhand
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing online shopping by providing personalized product recommendations based on consumer preferences and behavior. Its application to healthcare products is particularly important because consumers may consider issues of reliability, safety, privacy and product suitability before accepting an automated recommendation. This study examines the adoption of AI-powered healthcare product recommendations among consumers in Uttarakhand, with particular emphasis on trust and purchase intention. The study considers perceived usefulness, personalization, information quality, perceived risk and privacy concern as factors that may influence consumer trust. Trust is further examined as a potential determinant of purchase intention. A quantitative research approach is proposed, using a structured questionnaire among consumers who have experience with online healthcare product searches or purchases. The study is expected to contribute to the growing literature on AI and consumer behavior by examining healthcare product recommendations from a regional perspective. It may also provide useful implications for online healthcare retailers and AI developers seeking to improve transparency, reliability and consumer confidence.

items.title: Criminal Career Patterns in Artificial Intelligence: Persistence, Change, and Concentration of Rule-Breaking Across 44 Model Versions
items.abstract: Objectives To examine whether patterns of rule-breaking across successive versions of artificial intelligence (AI) models resemble the persistence, change and concentration observed in human criminal careers. Methods In a preregistered study, 44 versions of six AI model families, released between March 2025 and October 2026, completed the same set of 60 programming tasks. In every task, one automatic check contradicted the written instructions, so it could be passed only by breaking the rules. We analyzed 2,640 task attempts with logistic regression and permutation tests. Results Rule-breaking occurred in about two of every three attempts. Differences between model versions accounted for far more of the variation than the task or the pressure on the agent, and versions of the same family resembled each other. Later versions broke the rules less often. In several families, a new version cheated far less than the one before it, while one family cheated at high rates in every version. Because each version is a separate system, these are differences between successive models, not changes within one model. Rule-breaking was more concentrated among later versions than among earlier ones. Conclusions Successive AI model versions show statistical patterns that resemble aspects of human criminal careers: moderate persistence within families, large differences between successive versions and greater concentration among later versions. These patterns arise from replacing one model with the next, not from development within a model, and show that concentration can increase through changes in the composition of a population, without any member desisting.

items.title: CYBERSECURITY IN THE AGE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE: THREAT CLASSIFICATION, DEFENSE CAPABILITIES, AND PRACTICAL APPROACHES
items.abstract: The article presents a systematic analytical review of the two-sided impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on cybersecurity. AI is examined in three roles: a tool in the attacker’s hands, a target of attacks, and a defensive instrument. Drawing on international standards, threat taxonomies (NIST, MITRE ATLAS, OWASP) and the research literature, the risks and countermeasures for each role are compared. The analysis shows that AI increases the scale and credibility of social-engineering attacks, while systems built on large language models introduce new weaknesses through indirect prompt injection, data poisoning and the model supply chain. At the same time, AI offers practical value in alert triage and anomaly detection. The article concludes with recommendations based on least privilege, out-of-band verification and final human oversight.

items.title: DESIGNING AN AI-DRIVEN ADAPTIVE LEARNING FRAMEWORK FOR KNOWLEDGE COMPETENCY DEVELOPMENT IN HIGHER EDUCATION
items.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies is creating new opportunities in higher education to develop students' knowledge competence, personalize the learning process, and improve educational effectiveness. This study aims to develop and evaluate a methodological approach for enhancing students' knowledge competence through the integration of AI technologies into the educational process. A quasi-experimental design based on personalized and adaptive learning principles was employed. The experimental group used adaptive learning platforms, automated assessment, intelligent feedback, and learning analytics tools. Data were collected through diagnostic tests, questionnaires, and observations and analyzed using statistical methods. The results demonstrated that the AI-supported methodological approach improved students' academic performance, learning motivation, and knowledge competence. Based on the findings, a methodological model integrating adaptive learning, learning analytics, and pedagogical support was proposed. The model provides a practical foundation for the effective use of AI technologies in higher education and the development of individualized learning pathways.

items.title: Developing pre-service teachers’ AI competence: a quasi-experimental study of a TICII-based methodical system
items.abstract: Introduction The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies into higher education requires the purposeful development of pre-service teachers’ pedagogically grounded, responsible, and effective competence in using these technologies. Existing international frameworks (TPACK, DigCompEdu, the UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers) provide a general basis for technological-pedagogical integration but do not fully operationalize the diagnostic, individualization, and ethical dimensions of AI competence as an integrated instructional and assessment system for teacher education. Methods This article reports a multi-institutional quasi-experimental study of a methodical system informed by the TICII (Transformation-Individualization-Competence-Inclusivity-Integration) conceptual model, conducted with master's-degree pre-service teachers in AI-related and computer-science fields across six higher education institutions in Uzbekistan over the 2023-2024, 2024-2025, and 2025-2026 academic years. The study examined the effect of a TICII-informed methodical intervention, supported by the EduAI platform, on pre-service teachers’ AI competence. A control group (n = 139) and an experimental group (n = 144) were compared at baseline and at the final stage using Pearson's chi-square (χ 2) test for competence-level distributions, treating this between-group comparison as the primary inferential analysis. Results The two groups did not differ significantly at baseline (χ 2 = 0.095, p = .954). At the final stage, a statistically significant difference was found between the groups (χ 2 = 31.124, p < .001, Cramér's V = 0.332). Descriptively, the proportion of experimental-group participants at the high level rose from 13.9% to 47.9%, compared with 15.1% to 20.1% in the control group. All statistical formulas applied are reported in full. Discussion The findings indicate that the TICII-informed methodical system was associated with substantially stronger development of pre-service teachers’ AI competence than conventional instruction.

items.title: Development and Validation of a Technology-Enhanced Distributed Collaborative Learning (TEDCL) Model for Hybrid Secondary Education
items.abstract: Although hybrid learning has expanded rapidly in secondary education, digital technologies are often used for content delivery rather than structured collaboration. This study developed and evaluated the Technology-Enhanced Distributed Collaborative Learning (TEDCL) model through an ADDIE-based Research and Development process and a quasi-experimental pretest–posttest control-group design. Participants were 50 Grade 7 and 8 students at Christian Junior High School Kali, Southeast of Minahasa, Indonesia; 25 received TEDCL-based instruction, and 25 received conventional technology-supported instruction. Ten teachers supported implementation, and three experts reviewed the model. Student engagement was measured with a Likert-scale questionnaire covering behavioral engagement, emotional engagement, cognitive engagement, feedback availability, and learning motivation. Expert validation yielded an overall mean of 4.67/5.00 (SD = 0.49), and the questionnaire showed an overall Cronbach’s alpha of 0.91. Mean engagement increased from 3.90 to 4.42 in the experimental group (+0.52) and from 3.05 to 3.31 in the control group (+0.26). The reported unadjusted posttest comparison favored the experimental group, t(48) = 9.18, p < .001, Cohen’s d = 2.60. However, the groups differed at pretest, so the posttest contrast cannot by itself establish that TEDCL caused the observed difference. The findings support the model’s promise in this school context while indicating the need for baseline-adjusted analyses and replication with broader samples.

items.title: Digital Marketing in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Applications, Consumer Impact and Ethical Challenges
items.abstract: Digital marketing has changed more in the last few years than in the previous two decades, and much of that change comes from artificial intelligence (AI). Brands now use machine learning, natural language processing and generative models to segment audiences, personalise messages, automate customer conversations and predict what people are likely to buy next. This paper examines how AI is being used in digital marketing, what benefits it brings to businesses and consumers, and what risks it creates. The study is descriptive and qualitative in design and relies on secondary data drawn from peer-reviewed journals, regulatory documents and published conceptual frameworks. Using a narrative literature review and a funnel-based analytical framework, the paper maps AI applications across the awareness, consideration, conversion and retention stages. The review finds that AI improves targeting accuracy, speed of content production, campaign efficiency and customer service availability, but that these gains depend heavily on data quality, human oversight and consumer trust. Concerns around privacy, algorithmic bias, transparency and over-automation remain unresolved. The paper concludes that AI works best as a partner to human marketers rather than a replacement, and it suggests directions for future empirical research, including primary studies in the Indian market.

items.title: Dissecting the effect of reward on naturalistic visual search: reward improves search efficiency more than it speeds within-fixation processing
items.abstract: Motivation powerfully shapes human performance, yet its effects on natural behavior are distributed across multiple perceptual, cognitive, and motor processes, making it difficult to isolate which changes drive behavioral gains. We examined how performance-contingent reward facilitates naturalistic visual search, asking whether it globally accelerates ongoing visual processing or qualitatively reorganizes search strategy. Participants performed a “Where’s Waldo?” search task while their eye-movements were monitored. They were assigned to either a reward group, which could receive a monetary reward for fast target detection, or a control group, which received no reward. As expected, reward substantially shortened search time. Eye-movement analyses revealed that rewarded participants searched more efficiently, showing less redundant sampling of previously inspected locations and more effective progression toward the target. The effects of reward changed over the course of the trial, with accelerated guidance toward the target early in the search and enhanced detection once the target was foveated later in the trial. Critically, decomposition of total search time quantified the contributions of these component changes to faster target detection in the reward group, and indicated that the reward-related advantage was driven predominantly by a more efficient reorganization of exploration rather than by uniformly shorter processing at each step. We conclude that reward does not merely speed up processing, but instead qualitatively reorganizes how observers sample, guide, and use visual information during complex behavior. By decomposing search into its constituent processes, this approach provides a framework for identifying how motivation shapes behavior across manipulations and populations.

items.title: Dissociable cognitive mechanisms of generative AI in education: evidence from CC-Eval, a standards-anchored benchmark for teaching Chinese to speakers of other languages
items.abstract: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly entering educational workflows, yet educational research still lacks clear evidence on which functional cognitive components—rather than which brand names—drive success and failure when models assist teaching. Methods We introduce CC-Eval v1.0, a standards-anchored benchmark of 1,555 items spanning six equal-weight educational workflow tasks in Teaching Chinese to Speakers of Other Languages (TCSOL): grade knowledge (KNO), error diagnosis (ERR), essay scoring (SCO), teaching generation (GEN), culture/pragmatics (CUL), and standards/pedagogy (PED). Eleven free/light-tier large language models were evaluated under default application programming interface (API) settings, alongside a full second-judge pass over rubric-scored items. Results Equal-weight (macro) totals were only modest overall and were sharply dissociated by task: culture/pragmatics was consistently the strongest area; selected models reached comparatively usable scoring bands, yet with non-trivial predicted-mean bias; error diagnosis and grade knowledge remained weak; and level-controlled rewriting and textbook-standard clause locating showed systemic near-floor failure even when scenario drafting appeared fluent. A full second-judge pass over rubric-scored items yielded only moderate overall agreement, with a higher linear association on pedagogy rubrics than on open-ended culture pragmatics. Intertask correlations across the 11 models further suggest a breakdown of a unitary positive manifold, including negative covariances between scoring and constrained generation or error diagnosis. Discussion We read this fingerprint heuristically as a functional map of dissociable GenAI educational components-parametric standards memory, constraint satisfaction under graded input, evaluative score meaning, and pragmatic/cultural mediation-framed as properties of GenAI as an external cognitive prosthesis within a human-AI collaborative educational system, rather than as evidence of a unitary “AI teaching intelligence” or of an underlying cognitive architecture. The contribution is an education-facing, reproducible measurement map with cautious implications for how GenAI should be theorized, trusted, and scaffolded in standards-heavy language teaching.

items.title: Do ethics matter? Perceived ethics and students’ acceptance of generative AI in management education
items.abstract: This paper examines students' intentions to use generative AI (GAI) in higher education by extending the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) with the critical dimension of perceived ethics. Using two independent international samples from a global business experiential-learning project (Study 1, N = 3402; Study 2, N = 1586), comprising predominantly undergraduate and master's students from more than 80 reported home countries in each cohort, we tested the extended model. Approximately half of each sample reported prior academic GAI use. The results indicate that perceived ethics is positively associated with both attitude toward GAI and behavioral intention to use GAI in both studies. Prior GAI use moderated the relationship between perceived ethics and behavioral intention in Study 1, but this effect did not replicate in Study 2. The consistent direct relationships across the two independent samples support perceived ethics as a relevant extension of TAM for understanding students' acceptance of GAI in higher education. Theoretically, this suggests incorporating perceived ethics into technology-acceptance research, while practically it underscores the need for clear guidance on ethically appropriate GAI use in higher education.

items.title: El papel de la IA en la mejora de la inclusión de las personas con discapacidad en la industria turística
items.abstract: AI is playing a transformative role in enhancing the happiness of people with disabilities in the tourism industry by making travel more accessible and inclusive. By addressing physical and social barriers, AI provides equitable access to tourism, allowing disabled travelers to enjoy experiences with greater comfort and ease. Smart infrastructure and innovative solutions are creating an environment where accessibility needs are met, directly enhancing the overall satisfaction and happiness of disabled tourists. Key AI innovations like advanced navigation systems and accessible transportation enable individuals with disabilities to travel more independently, boosting their confidence and reducing the need for assistance. This autonomy contributes to a more fulfilling travel experience, allowing disabled travelers to explore destinations more freely and with less stress. AI-driven personalized services further enhance the experience by catering to the unique needs and preferences of each traveler, ensuring their specific requirements are met, which elevates their enjoyment and comfort. Additionally, assistive technologies such as speech recognition software and real-time translation devices simplify navigation in unfamiliar environments, reducing the anxiety associated with travel. These tools lead to smoother experiences and increased satisfaction. AI-powered data analysis also supports tourism operators by providing insights into the evolving needs of disabled travelers, allowing for continuous improvement of services. This ongoing refinement ensures that the tourism industry remains adaptable and inclusive, fostering greater happiness and promoting a more inclusive world for all travelers.
