items.title: Emerging Developments in Wearable Technologies for Healthcare: A Semi‐Automated Horizon Scan
items.abstract: Horizon scanning is a foresight methodology that supports the early identification and assessment of emerging developments, trends, risks, and evidence gaps to inform research, policy, and decision‐making. This study aimed to advance horizon scanning methodologies for emerging health technologies by evaluating the use of large language models (LLMs) to support filtration and data extraction within a live horizon scan of literature, funding portals, clinical trials, and patents. Using wearable technologies as a case study, LLM‐assisted workflows were evaluated within a human‐in‐the‐loop framework. LLM‐assisted filtration achieved high sensitivity across data sources and reduced the volume of records requiring manual review, while semi‐automated and automated extraction demonstrated high sensitivity across most evaluated variables. An Acceptability Profile was used to assess automation performance in relation to decision criticality, risk tolerance, safeguards, and intended use. Together, the findings demonstrate that LLM‐assisted automation can support horizon scanning workflows with appropriate validation and human oversight. The live horizon scan identified differences between innovation activity and clinical validation across wearable technology applications, a predominance of consumer devices, and limited evidence in certain populations, including children. Patient and public involvement highlighted considerations relating to usability, acceptability, trust, and likely real‐world adoption. This study provides a practical and transparent approach for implementing automation in horizon scanning to support timely and actionable evidence generation.

items.title: Emotionally supportive pedagogies and student wellbeing: the role of teacher empathy, classroom belongingness, and classroom emotional climate
items.abstract: Introduction Empathic teaching may support student wellbeing, but its effects may depend on classroom emotional climate. Drawing on self-determination theory, this study examined classroom belongingness as a mediating pathway and positive emotional climate as a moderator. Methods Two studies with Chinese university students used a 2 × 2 between-subjects video experiment independently manipulating teacher empathy and classroom emotional climate. Study 1 (N = 160) assessed manipulation effectiveness and stimulus comparability. Study 2 (N = 428) measured anticipated classroom belongingness immediately after exposure and psychological wellbeing (WHO-5) approximately two weeks later. Data were analysed in R using confirmatory factor analysis and baseline-adjusted conditional process models with 5,000 bootstrap resamples. Results Higher teacher empathy increased classroom belongingness under both climate conditions, with a larger effect under positive climate. Belongingness was positively associated with subsequent wellbeing. Conditional indirect effects were significant under both conditions and stronger under positive climate; the index of moderated mediation was 0.280 (95% bootstrap CI [0.065, 0.545]). Discussion Findings support a statistical indirect pathway from teacher empathy to subsequent wellbeing through anticipated classroom belongingness, strengthened by positive classroom emotional climate. Because the mediator was measured rather than experimentally manipulated, causal interpretation of the indirect effects is limited.

items.title: Employee Trust in Generative Artificial Intelligence–Enabled Corporate Social Responsibility Communication: Transparency, Human Oversight and Authenticity
items.abstract: This study investigates a framework integrating Stakeholder Theory, Signalling Theory, and Trust Theory to examine how CSR GenAI Disclosure Transparency (AIDT) and Perceived Human Oversight in GenAI‐Enabled CSR (PHO) are associated with Stakeholder Trust in GenAI‐Enabled CSR (ST). This study further investigates the statistical indirect associations through Stakeholder Empowerment Perception (SEP) and Perceived CSR Authenticity (PCSA). Data were collected from 330 respondents using a structured online survey administered through Prolific Academic and analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS‐SEM). The findings indicate that employees' perceptions of AI‐related CSR disclosure transparency and human oversight of GenAI‐enabled CSR were positively associated with stakeholder trust, both directly and indirectly through perceived stakeholder empowerment and CSR authenticity, respectively. This study contributes to responsible AI governance and GenAI‐enabled CSR communication research by identifying distinct indirect associations linking transparency with trust through empowerment and human oversight with trust through authenticity.

items.title: Empowering Socially Sustainable Mobility: How Intrinsic Motivations Shape the Intention to Adopt Intelligent Vehicle Automation Feature Sets for Diverse User Groups
items.abstract: The sustainable intention of using intelligent vehicles relies not only on technological advancement, but also on an explicit clarification of user intrinsic motivations. This study explores how cognitive, emotional, and behavioral empowerment shape drivers’ intentions to use intelligent vehicle automation features. Based on Delphi consultation and rigorous psychometric testing, we develop and validate a measurement scale and classify automated functions into three dimensions: smart interaction, vehicle control, and attention management. Using valid survey data from 614 drivers, the empirical results reveal that cognitive empowerment acts as the most powerful predictor of usage intention, surpassing the effects of emotional and behavioral empowerment. This study extends empowerment theory to human–vehicle interaction contexts and challenges the technology-dominated design paradigm that ignores user enablement. The findings provide user-centric design guidelines and policy references for fostering social and commercially sustainable intelligent mobility. However, we explicitly acknowledge that greater willingness to use automation features does not necessarily translate into realized environmental outcomes; linking feature engagement to broader social and commercial sustainability remains a critical avenue for future research.

items.title: Engaging university students with media theory through art-inspired creativity
items.abstract: The study investigates how creative activities including storyboarding, collaging, drawing, poetry writing, poster making, and basic cartography can engage students with abstract media concepts. Informed by Reeve and Tseng’s concept of ‘agentic engagement’ and Veiga et al.’s four-dimensional framework, and drawing on interviews with students and staff, the research explores how creativity, craftiness, and applied imagination can influence students’ engagement from a cognitive, behavioural, affective, and agentic perspective. The results, collected over a two-year period and examined through a dual-pronged approach, combining Thematic Analysis with Corpus-Assisted Discourse Analysis, indicate that creative pedagogies were commonly associated with students’ perceptions of their active contribution to the learning process, positioning creativity within an agentic dimension of engagement. The study demonstrates that creative affordances can enhance intellectual and active participation in class, and in supporting student learning. However, the implementation of creative activities may also face resistance among students, mostly due to self-consciousness and fear of judgement, which may inhibit spontaneous creative explorations. This article aims to spark a discussion over the benefits and challenges of using creativity to teach media concepts at university level, and to share tested ideas for whoever wishes to implement similar activities in their teaching.

items.title: Epistemic framing in AI-mediated university physics problem solving: a qualitative multiple-case study
items.abstract: Research on large language model-based generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in physics education has examined model performance, students’ evaluations of generated responses, and learning outcomes. Less is known about how generated explanations and calculations enter students’ observable physics problem-solving activity. This qualitative multiple-case study examines epistemic-frame sequences and their relation to solution quality, alongside students’ interactions with ChatGPT and their subsequent use of generated contributions. It analyses 30 submissions from 73 students across five university courses: 22 using ChatGPT and eight without it. ChatGPT was selected because its free version was students’ most frequently reported GenAI tool for independent study. Written artefacts and interaction records were analysed using Nguyen et al problem framing framework, with solution quality assessed independently. Activity recurrently moved between conceptual and algorithmic physics, but frame-sequence length did not distinguish solution quality. Challenges and reformulations made students’ evaluation of ChatGPT responses visible, whereas incorporation without documented evaluation sometimes carried generated errors into final submissions. The heterogeneous dataset confines interpretation to qualitative patterns and precludes causal comparison. The findings identify students’ observable evaluation and use of generated responses as a key link between GenAI output and documented physics reasoning.

items.title: Factors associated with teachers' adoption of Artificial Intelligence in Vietnamese high schools
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) adoption in high school History teaching remains underexamined. This study assessed associations among AI awareness (AAI), attitudes toward AI use (AAIU), technical support and resources (TSR), organizational culture and environment (OCE), practical application (PA), and teachers’ perceived impacts on students and learning outcomes (ISLO). An online survey yielded 335 responses from Vietnamese high school History teachers with prior AI-use experience; 17 incomplete or invalid cases were excluded, leaving 318 responses for partial least squares structural equation modeling. All eight prespecified direct paths were positive and statistically significant. The strongest associations were PA with ISLO (β = 0.599), AAI with AAIU (β = 0.597), and TSR with PA (β = 0.445). Significant specific indirect associations were also observed through AAIU, TSR, and PA. The model explained 66.2% of the variance in AAIU, 38.5% in TSR, 61.9% in PA, and 68.8% in ISLO. Because the data were single-source, self-reported, and cross-sectional, the results do not establish causality or objective student learning effects. The study provides a context-specific application of general AI-adoption constructs and highlights the relevance of teacher development, technical resources, and school-level support for responsible AI use in Vietnamese high school History teaching.

items.title: FigmaEval: A Benchmark for Evaluating AI Agents in Professional UI Design
items.abstract: Recent advances in AI agents have enabled autonomous UI design using professional tools such as Figma, yet evaluating their design capabilities remains challenging due to the open-ended nature of design tasks and the absence of unique ground truths. We introduce FigmaEval, a benchmark for evaluating AI agents on professional UI design tasks, comprising 84 tasks and 783 screens derived from real-world Figma design files. FigmaEval adopts a constrained-specification, open-solution paradigm, standardizing task requirements and design resources while allowing agents to independently determine layouts, visual hierarchies, component composition, and visual presentation. To assess design quality beyond reference similarity, we develop 22 expert-grounded evaluation rubrics across six dimensions and introduce a human evaluation arena where professional designers compare agent-generated designs through blinded pairwise judgments. Evaluating eleven models under a unified Figma agent setup, we find substantial agreement between rubric-based assessments and human preferences, alongside distinct differences in design practices and quality--efficiency trade-offs. FigmaEval provides a framework for systematically assessing professional UI design capabilities and understanding the strengths and limitations of current AI agents.

items.abstract: Foundation models may increase healthcare robots' autonomy and adaptability, but they also connect model vulnerabilities and cyberattacks to physical and health-system harm. We propose a stage-gated framework assigning assurance activities to manufacturers, healthcare organizations, and clinical teams from design through post-market monitoring.

items.title: From AI Explanations to Human Decisions: A Structured Literature Review and Governance Taxonomy for Enterprise and Supply Chain Decision Support
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in enterprise and supply chain decision support, yet explanation availability alone does not guarantee informed human decisions.This structured literature review critically connects research on explainable AI, human-AI collaboration, organizational adoption, and governance.It proposes an Explanation-to-Decision Governance (EDG) Taxonomy comprising five analytical dimensions: AI explanation, human interpretation, decision authority, crosscutting governance controls, and operational outcomes.Drawing on selected scholarly literature and governance guidance, the paper distinguishes explanation comprehensibility from verifiability, appropriate reliance, and authorized intervention.It illustrates how the taxonomy can frame decisions in forecasting, inventory planning, and exception management and proposes evaluation questions for future research.The synthesis is narrative and selective rather than exhaustive: no complete database screening, reproducible corpus, or PRISMA flow counts are claimed.The EDG Taxonomy remains a conceptual contribution requiring independent empirical validation.

items.title: From AI Literacy to Employee Performance: A Systematic Review of Learning and Training Transfer
items.abstract: Effective workplace use of artificial intelligence (AI) requires employees to identify appropriate tasks, critically evaluate AI-generated outputs, and exercise professional judgment. However, the extent to which AI-related competencies acquired through training are transferred to everyday workplace practices and contribute to improved employee performance remains unclear. This systematic review examined how employee AI literacy was measured, developed through professional training, and associated with training transfer and job performance. Peer-reviewed empirical studies published between 2019 and October 2026 were identified through searches conducted using two web search engines and supplementary reference screening. Methodological quality was assessed using the 2018 Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT). Given the heterogeneity of measurement approaches and research designs, the findings were synthesized thematically. The review included 43 empirical reports, of which 10 evaluated professional training programs. AI literacy was assessed using self-reported measures, objective knowledge tests, and proxy indicators derived from professional experience or employee profiles. Training programs commonly incorporated practical exercises, project-based learning, and reflective activities to develop AI-related competencies. Although several studies reported the application of acquired skills in workplace settings, evidence of sustained training transfer and long-term competency utilization remained limited. Variations in outcome measures and the predominance of nonrandomized research designs constrained the ability to establish whether AI literacy directly improved employee performance. Based on these findings, the review proposed a conceptual framework linking professional training, AI literacy development, training transfer, and job performance. Future research should empirically examine these relationships through longitudinal workplace assessments and independent, objective performance indicators, including task quality, task completion time, and error rates.

items.title: From Decision Support to Delegated Clinical Action: Governing the Autonomy Gradient of AI-Driven Clinical Decision Support Systems
items.abstract: AI-driven clinical decision support systems can prepare executable orders, communicate with patients, and initiate multistep workflows, raising unresolved questions about delegated clinical authority. This viewpoint proposes a 5-level clinical autonomy gradient: informational support (A0), advisory decision support (A1), human-confirmed execution (A2), bounded delegated action (A3), and adaptive autonomous management (A4). Classification applies to a task-action pair within its deployment workflow. Execution authority and case-specific human authorization anchor assignment; decision influence, temporal reach, and scope adaptability describe the configuration. The action-enablement boundary (A1-A2) introduces executable action preparation requiring explicit, informed, case-specific authorization before release. The delegation boundary (A2-A3) permits execution without contemporaneous, case-specific authorization. We adapt an automation scope of practice to record permissions and operating conditions, and an autonomy safety case to link authority to deployment-specific evidence and residual risks. Proposed controls address effective human review, interacting systems, proportionate governance, and withholding, downgrading, or suspending actions when supporting conditions fail. Applications to documented systems and hypothetical scenarios illustrate classification reasoning without establishing reliability or delegated-action safety. Greater autonomy is optional; A1 or A2 may remain appropriate. Independent evaluation must assess classification agreement, feasibility, implementation burden, and effects on care.

items.title: From Language Teacher to Educational Developer: An Analytic Autoethnography of Human–AI Collaboration in English Language Education
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming educational practice, yet existing research has limited attention to how sustained human–AI collaboration reshapes teachers’ professional capabilities. This study employed analytic autoethnography to examine the professional journey of an English language teacher who collaborated with generative AI to design and develop multiple educational applications, including digital assessment systems, customised learning management system extensions, vocabulary learning tools, and AI-assisted language learning applications. Data consisted of reflective journals, AI interaction logs, development artefacts, and implementation records, which were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. The findings reveal that authentic pedagogical problems initiated iterative cycles of human–AI collaboration and continued to the simultaneous development of technological and pedagogical capabilities that culminated in educational innovation and professional identity transformation. Based on these findings, the study proposes the Teacher Capability Transformation through Human–AI Collaboration (TCT-HAIC) Model, which conceptualises teacher capability development as a cyclical process driven by authentic educational challenges followed by sustained collaboration with AI. The study contributes a novel perspective by positioning generative AI not merely as an instructional tool but as a collaborative partner that expands teachers’ capabilities for continuous professional learning and educational innovation.

items.title: From naïve certainty to intellectual humility: how an AI-SSI curriculum reshapes high school students’ socioscientific orientations
items.abstract: This study examines the effects of an ENACT model-guided, Artificial Intelligence-related Socioscientific Issues (AI-SSI) curriculum on high school students’ socioscientific orientations (SO). While SSI-based pedagogy is recognized for enhancing scientific literacy and moral development, its specific effects within the domain of AI ethics remain underexplored. Employing a mixed-methods pretest-posttest design, this research investigated the influence of a 10-week AI-SSI intervention on 45 Chinese tenth-graders’ SO. Findings revealed significant pre-to-post declines in self-reported SO across all four dimensions --- ecological worldview, social and moral compassion, socioscientific accountability, and scientific evidence views. However, qualitative interview data suggest that these declines reflect epistemic development and the emergence of intellectual humility: students transitioned from simplistic, absolutist views toward more nuanced, conditional, and critical understandings of AI-SSI dilemmas. These findings imply that initial decreases in self-reported competencies may signal deeper epistemic development, including enhanced critical reasoning and more calibrated self-awareness of complexity. This study underscores the need for assessment strategies that can capture such intricate cognitive transformations. Overall, the findings suggest that AI-SSI instruction, when implemented under supportive conditions, has the potential to foster intellectual humility and nuanced ethical reasoning—dispositions that are important for navigating an AI-saturated world. These findings offer preliminary implications for AI-SSI, civic literacy, and responsible innovation.

items.title: From Replacement to Augmentation: A Human-Centered Framework for Consumer Robots
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence and related hardware and software technologies have accelerated the development of consumer robots, creating new opportunities for robots to support people in everyday life. However, advanced technology is only the foundation for achieving this goal. A complete design concept for robots aimed at ordinary consumers is also needed. This paper examines the importance of positioning consumer robots as tools for human augmentation, the reason why consumer robot interaction design should mainly use intuitive operation, and the safety issues that influence user trust and acceptance. The analysis argues that consumer robots should prioritize human augmentation rather than complete robot autonomy. This approach protects consumer control while giving users stronger capabilities. In addition, robot products can only be psychologically accepted when consumers trust them. To achieve this positioning, intuitive interaction can reduce the barriers for ordinary consumers and allow more natural interaction. Products should also provide data privacy protection, control-right protection, and safety that can be perceived by users. The significance of this paper is that it provides a consumer-centered design framework for robots aimed at ordinary consumers.

items.title: Gamification in the age of AI: surveying player perceptions of motivation, manipulation, and data protection
items.abstract: Modern games and applications increasingly employ artificial intelligence (AI), user modeling, and gamification to influence user behavior, sustain engagement, and monetize attention. Although these mechanisms can enhance motivation and enjoyment, they also raise concerns about manipulation, personal data usage, and transparency. To examine how players perceive these dynamics, we conducted a survey with 28 adult participants. Respondents expressed strong concerns about the collection and exploitation of personal information in games and gamified applications, while also reporting low awareness and a limited sense of control over how their data is used. They evaluated progression features such as leveling systems and leaderboards as motivating. In contrast, they rated retention-focused mechanics such as daily login rewards and random reward reveals as highly manipulative. Participants reported that these systems can create fear of missing out or resemble gambling. Participants also expressed support for regulatory measures that limit exploitative design and protect vulnerable users. These findings reveal a clear gap between increasingly powerful engagement strategies and user trust, illustrating the need for more responsible and transparent gamification practices.

items.title: Generative AI Reliance, Developer Skill Atrophy, and Late-Stage Project Risk: A Mediation Analysis of Software Engineering Teams
items.abstract: While generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) coding assistants accelerate initial code generation, their downstream consequences for practitioner skill retention and software delivery stability remain underexplored. Drawing on cognitive load theory, automation bias theory, and technical debt theory, this study investigates how developer skill atrophy (DSA) mediates the relationship between generative AI reliance (GAIR) and late-stage project risk and technical defect escalation (LPR) across a sample of active software engineering practitioners (N = 142). Ordinary least squares (OLS) regressions and a 5,000-resample non-parametric bootstrap mediation model reveal a statistically significant competitive dual-path mechanism. Specifically, habitual reliance on GenAI strongly predicts developer skill atrophy (β* = .619, p < .001), which in turn strongly predicts late-stage project risk (β* = .672, p < .001). The indirect mediation pathway through skill atrophy is substantial and positive (a*b* = .502, 95% Boot CI [.338, .588], p < .001). Conversely, once skill atrophy is held constant, direct GenAI reliance exhibits a statistically significant protective effect against late-stage project risk (β* = -.228, p = .002), yielding a net positive total effect (c = .249, p = .025). Qualitative practitioner reflections (n = 48) corroborate these findings, highlighting superficial code reviews, degraded mental execution models, and late-sprint integration bottlenecks. These results resolve the productivity-versus-risk paradox of GenAI adoption and demonstrate that AI coding tools improve delivery reliability only when paired with deliberate verification and skill-retention practices. items.title: GENERATIVE AI-MEDIATED ORAL ENGLISH LEARNING IN TECHNICAL EDUCATION: EFFECTIVENESS, OPPORTUNITIES AND PEDAGOGICAL CHALLENGES
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has created new opportunities for oral English practice, but evidence specific to post-secondary technical education remains limited. This paper examines the effectiveness, instructional opportunities and pedagogical challenges reported in a bounded set of studies involving diploma and polytechnic learners. A structured scoping-review-informed search covered publications from 1January 2022 to 31 October 2026. Five accessible bibliographic exports yielded 4,007 rows, reduced to 3,756 records after preliminary deduplication. As the wider corpus was not fully screened, the evidence set was frozen on 1 November 2026. Three full-text-verified primary studies were synthesised, while one mixed-tool study was used for implementation context only. The strongest comparative study reported an overall posttest speaking advantage for the GenAI-supported group (Hedges’ g = 0.63, p = .003); however, only interaction remained significant after correction for multiple comparisons. Other studies described benefits for speaking-task preparation, dialogue practice and confidence, alongside mixed performance results, overreliance and methodological limitations. GenAI may therefore supplement teacher-guided oral English instruction, particularly when activities are linked to technical communication and followed by independent speaking tasks. The findings are illustrative rather than exhaustive, and do not establish a general causal effect on oral proficiency.

items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence in English Language Learning: A Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: This systematic literature review explores how Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is being used in English language learning and what effects it has on students' language skills, motivation, and overall learning journey. GenAI refers to intelligent systems that can create written content, simulate conversations, and provide instant help to learners — tools that have become increasingly noticeable since 2020 as helpful resources for reading, writing, speaking, and vocabulary practice. While many people are excited about these technologies, research findings still show mixed results. There are ongoing concerns about how accurate the information is, whether learners might depend too heavily on AI, how it affects independent thinking skills, and what constitutes proper use. For this review, twenty-three research papers published between 2020 and 2026 were examined, using a thematic approach to bring together the key insights. Studies were selected based on how closely they relate to English teaching, the quality of their research methods, and whether they specifically looked at real GenAI applications in language learning. The results show that, generally, GenAI helps improve writing quality, builds speaking confidence, keeps learners more engaged, and makes practice opportunities more accessible. However, the evidence also leans heavily toward higher education and writing tasks, with less known about long-term results. Key challenges include the risk of over-reliance, possible impacts on critical thinking, and unequal access across different learner groups. This review concludes that GenAI has real potential to support language learning but it works best when used alongside clear teaching strategies and ethical guidelines. Based on these findings, recommendations suggest that schools and teachers create structured guidelines for responsible GenAI use, and that future research expands across more diverse educational settings to ensure these tools truly benefit all learners fairly.

items.title: Global Automation Atlas
items.abstract: Whether automation can replace or support workers depends not only on task content, but also on the conditions under which work is performed. Existing exposure measures typically assign fixed scores to tasks, capturing country differences only through employment structure. We use a large language model to classify 18,797 tasks in 124 economies by feasible exposure, labour substitution or augmentation, technology type and reliance on artificial intelligence. Accounting for country conditions changes occupation rankings and improves predictions of firms’ technology use. Exposure ranges from 3.3% to 61.6% of tasks and rises with income. Lower-income economies have fewer exposed tasks, but exposure is more concentrated in rule-based, labour-substituting automation, whereas labour-augmenting uses of artificial intelligence become more prominent with development. Women are disproportionately employed in occupations exposed to labour substitution. Model rationales for exposure more often mention machinery, digital records and connected systems, whereas rationales for non-exposure point to local knowledge and trusted relationships.

items.title: Governing LLM decision authority in tourism: A bounded generative agency framework for multi-stakeholder itinerary planning
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly support tourism itinerary decisions, yet factual grounding alone cannot establish whether a recommendation is acceptable to stakeholders or feasible to implement. This study develops SilverRoute, a framework integrating LLMs, geographic information systems (GIS), and multicriteria decision analysis. Under bounded generative agency, the LLM interprets needs and explains outcomes, while spatial evidence and formal rules govern feasibility, stakeholder acceptability, coordination, and recommendation or abstention. Evaluation used 4,750 facility and service features, 5,459 road features, and 698 cultural points of interest across 48 age-friendly tourism planning scenarios in Ya'an, China. An evidence-grounded LLM achieved 100% factual-claim accuracy but only 45.14% protocol alignment and recommended routes in all eight infeasible cases. Bounding its authority raised alignment to 100% and eliminated inappropriate and forced recommendations. In 40 recommendable scenarios, SilverRoute respected all stakeholder acceptability boundaries, whereas scalar baselines crossed at least one boundary in 17.5-20.0% of cases. Ablations showed that screening acceptability before aggregation provided most of the protection, while Nash bargaining became more consequential as preferences diverged. Time-boundary and repair tests showed that abstention can identify the requirement blocking action and support planner-confirmed adjustments without relaxing protected thresholds. The findings show how explicitly allocating decision rights can make itinerary planning auditable while supporting personalization and protecting stakeholder requirements.
